relevance_reason: Case report of an infant with cation-leaky GLUT1 deficiency (stomatin-deficient cryohydrocytosis with neurologic defects) caused by an SLC2A1 in-frame deletion.

findings.statement: Bawazir et al. (2012) described an infant with GLUT1 deficiency and a cation-leaky red cell state who presented with erratic hyperkalemia, neonatal hyperbilirubinemia, anemia, hepatic dysfunction, and microcephaly. Later, seizures occurred and developmental milestones were delayed. Brain MRI and CT showed multiple abnormalities, including periventricular calcification, and visual impairment resulted from cataracts and retinal dysfunction.
quotes: The infant presented with erratic hyperkalemia, neonatal hyperbilirubinemia, anemia, hepatic dysfunction, and microcephaly. Later, seizures occurred and developmental milestones were delayed.
Magnetic resonance imaging and computerized tomography scans of the brain showed multiple abnormalities including periventricular calcification.
Visual impairment was present due to the presence of both cataracts and retinal dysfunction.

findings.statement: Bawazir et al. (2012) found that the patient's red cells were extremely leaky to cations, which caused the hemolysis. Red cells lost potassium in a temperature-dependent way, which explained the hyperkalemia as pseudohyperkalemia.
quotes: Measurements of red cell cation content showed extremely leaky red cells (causing the hemolysis) and temperature-dependent loss of potassium from red cells (explaining the hyperkalemia as pseudohyperkalemia).

findings.statement: In the proband, Bawazir et al. (2012) identified a trinucleotide deletion in the SLC2A1 gene that deletes isoleucine 435 or 436 of GLUT1. They noted that this was the fourth pedigree reported with this syndrome.
quotes: A trinucleotide deletion in SLC2A1, coding for the deletion of isoleucine 435 or 436 in GLUT1, was identified in the proband.
This is the fourth pedigree to be described with this most unusual syndrome.

variants.as_reported: trinucleotide deletion coding for the deletion of isoleucine 435 or 436

findings.statement: Bawazir et al. (2012) suggested that the multisystem pathology probably reflects two effects: deficient glucose transport at the blood-brain barrier, as in typical GLUT1 deficiency, and the harmful osmotic effects of a cation-leaky membrane protein in cells that express GLUT1, notably red cells.
quotes: The multisystem pathology probably reflects a combination of glucose transport deficiency at the blood-brain barrier (as in typical GLUT1 deficiency) and the deleterious osmotic effects of a cation-leaky membrane protein in the cells where GLUT1 is expressed, notably the red cell.

relevance_reason: Identifies SLC2A1 mutations as the cause of stomatin-deficient cryohydrocytosis with neurologic features, with functional studies in Xenopus oocytes.

findings.statement: Flatt et al. (2011) noted that they had previously reported 2 cases of stomatin-deficient cryohydrocytosis (sdCHC), a rare form of stomatocytosis associated with a cold-induced cation leak, hemolytic anemia, and hepatosplenomegaly, as well as cataracts, seizures, mental retardation, and movement disorder.
quotes: We have previously reported 2 cases of stomatin-deficient cryohydrocytosis (sdCHC), a rare form of stomatocytosis associated with a cold-induced cation leak, hemolytic anemia, and hepatosplenomegaly but also with cataracts, seizures, mental retardation, and movement disorder.

findings.statement: In the 2 patients with stomatin-deficient cryohydrocytosis, Flatt et al. (2011) identified 2 different mutations in the SLC2A1 gene. Expression studies in Xenopus oocytes showed that the mutations caused both loss of glucose transport and a cation leak. On the basis of a 3-dimensional model of GLUT1, the authors proposed potential mechanisms underlying the phenotypes of the 2 mutations.
quotes: We now show that sdCHC is associated with mutations in SLC2A1 that cause both loss of glucose transport and a cation leak, as shown by expression studies in Xenopus oocytes.
On the basis of a 3-dimensional model of glut1, we propose potential mechanisms underlying the phenotypes of the 2 mutations found.

findings.statement: Flatt et al. (2011) found that loss of stomatin during erythropoiesis in sdCHC occurs during reticulocyte maturation and involves endocytosis.
quotes: We investigated the loss of stomatin during erythropoiesis and find this occurs during reticulocyte maturation and involves endocytosis.

relevance_reason: This paper reports the only two known patients with stomatin-deficient cryohydrocytosis. Both had mental retardation, seizures, cataracts and massive hepatosplenomegaly, and the authors proposed this as a new haemato-neurological syndrome.

findings.statement: Fricke et al. (2004) described 2 patients with stomatin-deficient cryohydrocytosis. In both, the passive red cell K+ leak was lowest at around 20 to 25 degrees C, so the cells were extremely leaky at 0 degrees C. Both had a congenital syndrome of mental retardation, seizures, cataracts and massive hepatosplenomegaly. The authors suggested that this probably defined a new haemato-neurological syndrome.
quotes: two showed a minimum at around 20-25 degrees C, such that the cells were extremely leaky at 0 degrees C, giving the phenotype known as 'cryohydrocytosis'

These patients are the only two known cases of stomatin-deficient cryohydrocytosis. Both showed a congenital syndrome of mental retardation, seizures, cataracts and massive hepatosplenomegaly, probably defining a new haemato-neurological syndrome.

findings.statement: Fricke et al. (2004) described 3 new isolated cases and 1 new pedigree of hereditary stomatocytosis, and gave further details on 1 previously reported case. In every case, Western blotting of red cell membranes showed a deficiency of stomatin, the 32-kD membrane protein. All cases had pronounced cation leaks at 37 degrees C, with markedly abnormal intracellular Na+ and K+ concentrations. Immunocytochemistry showed that the stomatin deficiency was not complete: some red cells were stomatin positive, and all platelets and neutrophils were stomatin positive.
quotes: In all cases, Western blotting of red cell membranes revealed a deficiency in the 32 kDa membrane protein, stomatin.
All showed pronounced cation leaks at 37 degrees C with markedly abnormal intracellular Na(+) and K(+) concentrations
immunocytochemistry demonstrated that the deficiency of stomatin was not complete
All platelets and neutrophils were stomatin positive.

findings.statement: Fricke et al. (2004) found that the stomatin-deficient cases differed markedly in how the passive K+ leak depended on temperature. Three cases showed a simple monotonic temperature dependence. The other 2 had a minimum at 20 to 25 degrees C, which is the cryohydrocytosis phenotype.
quotes: The cases differed markedly between themselves with regard to the temperature dependence of the passive leak to K(+). Three showed a simple monotonic temperature dependence

relevance_reason: The abstract reports that a band 7 erythrocyte membrane protein (22 x 8) was missing in one patient with cryohydrocytosis and one with hereditary stomatocytosis. It gives early biochemical evidence of stomatin (band 7) deficiency in cryohydrocytosis. It does not describe neurologic features.

findings.statement: Lande et al. (1982) studied erythrocyte membrane proteins from 2 patients with congenital hemolytic anemia caused by increased erythrocyte membrane permeability to Na and K: one had hereditary stomatocytosis and one had cryohydrocytosis. On one-dimensional SDS gel electrophoresis, the 28,000-dalton band 7 component was reduced in both patients. On two-dimensional electrophoresis, this component resolved into 2 proteins, 22 x 8 and 60 x 8. Protein 22 x 8 was completely absent in both patients, while 60 x 8 was present.
quotes: The 28,000-dalton component was decreased in both patients with permeability disorders.
In the patients with hereditary stomatocytosis and cryohydrocytosis, 22 x 8 was completely absent, whereas 60 x 8 was detected as usual.

phenotypes.text: increased erythrocyte membrane permeability to Na and K
absent band 7 erythrocyte membrane protein 22 x 8

findings.statement: Lande et al. (1982) found that all band 7 proteins, including 22 x 8, were present in every normal subject and reticulocytosis control they surveyed. Because the missing protein was unique to the patients, the authors raised the possibility that absence of this band 7 protein is responsible for the increased Na and K permeability in hereditary stomatocytosis and cryohydrocytosis.
quotes: In contrast, all the band 7 proteins (including 22 x 8) were invariably present in a survey of normal subjects and reticulocytosis controls.

The unique finding of a missing band 7 protein in the patients with hereditary stomatocytosis and cryohydrocytosis raises the possibility that the absence of this protein is responsible for the increased Na and K permeability in these disorders.
